# The Thirteenth Hand — complete script

<!-- Generated from src/story/*.ts by `npm run story:script`. Do not edit by hand: change the campaign data and regenerate. -->

Every scene of the campaign, in play order: each chapter’s arrival, each challenge’s scene before and after the game, the chapter’s departure, and the epilogue. The player is a silent observer — narration (in italics) speaks to them in the second person; they never speak.

Poses in brackets are the character’s expression for that line. **[Clue]** marks the moment a piece of evidence is added to the journal.

**History and legend.** Field notes marked _history_ are documented and give a source. Notes marked _about the story_ say what is invented. The ghosts, the card, Operation Thirteenth Hand, the tunnels and the unfinished game are fiction.

## Chapter 1: The Card Without a Suit

**Place:** Cheryl’s Antique Shop (fictional). **Host:** Cheryl. **Cast:** Cheryl. **Music:** lamplight.

_An estate-sale box, twelve old decks and one card that should not exist._

**The mystery so far:** The Thirteenth Hand card turns up in Lot 13 with a ledger of twelve recorded hands; its four corners are blank, waiting for suit marks. A postcard points to the River Station.

**Arrival**

> _You step into Cheryl’s Antique Shop. A bell rings over the door, and forty clocks disagree about the time._
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-neutral)_: We close at five. It’s ten to.
>
> _On the counter you see an estate-sale box tied with string, a twenty-dollar tag still on the knot. One card lies on top._
>
> **Cheryl** _(cards-reveal)_: Lot 13, from an estate sale across the river. Twelve old decks, a ledger, and that. A collector comes at nine for the decks.
>
> _You pick up the card. It has no suit and no number — only the words THE THIRTEENTH HAND, and four blank corners._ **[Clue: The Thirteenth Hand]**
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-doubt)_: Provenance is a story with receipts. That card has neither. Nobody prints a card without a suit unless they want it noticed.
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-talk)_: I don’t sell a lot I haven’t counted. Help me inventory it tonight, and you can look at anything in the box.

### 1.1 Price Check

**Game:** war against Cheryl. **Objective:** Win War against Cheryl. **Table:** fredericksburg deck on cheryls_antique_shop, deal 2007 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Cheryl** _(cards-deal)_: We split the twelve decks by War. High card picks. It’s faster than arguing.

**After the win**

> _Cheryl slides a receipt across the counter to you: Lot 13, one card box, contents as found._ **[Clue: Estate-sale receipt]**
>
> **Cheryl**: Lot thirteen. The auction house thought that was funny. I didn’t.

**Rewards:** 45 credits, 65 XP, clue: Estate-sale receipt.

### 1.2 Sorting the Box

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 1. **Table:** fredericksburg deck on cheryls_antique_shop, deal 1008 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _The box holds twelve loose decks, all shuffled together. Cheryl hands you one to sort._
>
> **Cheryl**: Aces up. A short deck sells for half. A complete one in its box sells for more than you’d think.

**After the win**

> _Under the decks you find a leather ledger. Twelve hands of cards are written out in faded ink. The thirteenth line is blank._ **[Clue: Ledger of twelve hands]**
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-think)_: Somebody kept score. And somebody stopped.
>
> **Cheryl**: One handwriting, twelve hands. That isn’t a game night. That’s a record.

**Rewards:** 55 credits, 75 XP, clue: Ledger of twelve hands.

### 1.3 Matched Sets

**Game:** go-fish against Cheryl. **Objective:** Win Go Fish against Cheryl. **Table:** fredericksburg deck on cheryls_antique_shop, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Cheryl** _(cards-shuffle)_: Go Fish. Don’t laugh. Asking for matches is the quickest way to find out a set is short.

**After the win**

> **Cheryl** _(portrait-think)_: Every deck in the box is complete. Fifty-two each. So the extra card didn’t come with them. Somebody added it.

**Rewards:** 65 credits, 85 XP.

### 1.4 The Locked Case

**Game:** freecell. **Objective:** FreeCell puzzle: finish the last four ranks. Use the free cells to plan ahead. **Table:** fredericksburg deck on cheryls_antique_shop, deal 1001 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _You notice that Cheryl’s display case has a puzzle lock: a FreeCell deal painted under the glass._
>
> **Cheryl**: My late husband’s idea of security. He said burglars don’t have the patience. He was right about most people.

**After the win**

> _You find an old postcard of the Rappahannock tucked in the box lid. A heron is sketched on the back, with two words: River Station._ **[Clue: River postcard]**
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-neutral)_: A heron and two words. That isn’t provenance either. But it’s a direction.

**Rewards:** 75 credits, 95 XP, clue: River postcard.

### 1.5 Under the Lamp (finale)

**Game:** spider. **Objective:** Finale: clear one-suit Spider. **Table:** fredericksburg deck on cheryls_antique_shop, deal 1035 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Cheryl**: Last one. Spider. Then we look at that card under a proper lamp. Daylight lies about paper.

**After the win**

> _You hold the card under the lamp. Its blank corners catch the light, each shaped for a suit mark — four of them, all missing._
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-think)_: Four empty corners. Somebody wants this card finished.

**Rewards:** 120 credits, 150 XP.

**Departure**

> **Cheryl**: River Station is Sophia’s. Parks and Rec. If anyone can tell you who stood at that bend and drew a heron, it’s her.
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-greet)_: I called the collector. Told him Monday. Take the card, bring it back, and get a receipt for anything you spend.
>
> _You tuck the card into your pocket and head for the river._

**Chapter rewards:** board: cheryls_antique_shop, passport stamp (Cheryl’s Antique Shop), achievement: passport-first, 300 credits, 200 XP.

**Chapter notes:**

- **Fredericksburg** (history): Fredericksburg was established in 1728 as a port on the Rappahannock River. Its historic downtown, including Caroline Street, is known today for its antique shops. Cheryl and her shop are fictional. _Source: City of Fredericksburg; Fredericksburg Area Museum._

## Chapter 2: The Heron’s Bend

**Place:** Rappahannock River Station (fictional). **Host:** Sophia. **Cast:** Sophia. **Music:** river-dawn.

_A heron sketch, a trail marker nobody remembers, Sophia’s river map and a letter that never reached Dante._

**The mystery so far:** The first suit mark — a club — is carved on an old trail marker at the heron’s bend. Sophia’s annotated river map shows four marks near the old waterfront, and a returned envelope ties the card to Dante.

**Arrival**

> _You follow the river path to the Rappahannock River Station. A heron stands in the shallows, unbothered._
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-greet)_: Morning. If you’re here about the heron, she’s fine. She’s fished that bend longer than I’ve worked here.
>
> _You show Sophia the postcard and the card._
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-think)_: That’s this bend. See the snag behind her? It washed in during the spring flood. Whoever drew this stood on our dock, and recently.
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-doubt)_: Last week a man with a phone on a stick filmed our lobby and asked for the visitor logs. Jak something. Constitutional right, he said. It was also my lunch break.
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-talk)_: I have a school group at two and a log to finish. Walk the route with me, and I’ll pull the sign-in sheets when we’re back.

### 2.1 Lunch Break

**Game:** go-fish against Sophia. **Objective:** Lay down 3 books against Sophia. **Table:** eastern_woodlands deck on rappahannock_riverside, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Sophia** _(cards-deal)_: Lunch break. Twenty minutes, and I’m eating. Go Fish is about all I can teach with one hand.

**After the win**

> _You read the wildlife log over Sophia’s shoulder: the same heron, at the same bend, every morning for years._ **[Clue: Field journal page]**
>
> **Sophia**: Consistent. Herons usually are. People aren’t.

**Rewards:** 50 credits, 70 XP, clue: Field journal page.

**Field notes:**

- **Great blue heron** (wildlife): The great blue heron is the largest heron in North America. It hunts by standing still in shallow water, then striking fast. Herons live along the Rappahannock all year. _Source: Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds._

### 2.2 Trail Markers

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 1. **Table:** eastern_woodlands deck on rappahannock_riverside, deal 3101 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _You walk the river trail with Sophia toward the heron’s bend._
>
> **Sophia**: Sort these while I check the markers. Half this job is noticing what moved overnight.

**After the win**

> _At the heron’s bend, an old trail marker leans toward the water. Carved into it is a small club — the exact size of one blank corner on your card._ **[Clue: The club mark]**
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-surprise)_: That marker is older than I am, and it isn’t on our trail inventory. Somebody set it where only high water reaches.

**Rewards:** 60 credits, 80 XP, clue: The club mark.

**Field notes:**

- **The fall line** (history): Fredericksburg grew where the Rappahannock drops over rocky rapids at the fall line — the farthest point ocean-going ships could sail upstream. The town was established in 1728 as a river port. _Source: City of Fredericksburg; Fredericksburg Area Museum._

### 2.3 The Archive Drawer

**Game:** go-fish against Sophia. **Objective:** Collect 3 books: choose your asks and remember the replies. **Table:** eastern_woodlands deck on rappahannock_riverside, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Sophia**: If that marker is old, it’s on an old map. The archive drawer sticks, and nobody’s labelled it since the nineties.

**After the win**

> _Sophia spreads her own annotated map of the river trail across the desk and lets you take it. Near the old waterfront, four small marks are circled in pencil._ **[Clue: Sophia’s annotated river map]**
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-think)_: Those four marks were on the survey I traced it from. They don’t match anything I know — and one of them is a club.

**Rewards:** 70 credits, 90 XP, clue: Sophia’s annotated river map.

**Field notes:**

- **American shad** (wildlife): Each spring, American shad swim up the Rappahannock from the ocean to spawn. Removing the Embrey Dam at Fredericksburg in 2004 reopened miles of river to them and other migrating fish. _Source: Friends of the Rappahannock; U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service._

### 2.4 High Water

**Game:** spider. **Objective:** Clear one-suit Spider. **Table:** eastern_woodlands deck on rappahannock_riverside, deal 1002 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Sophia**: River’s up, so the lower trail is closed. While it drops, the lost-and-found needs sorting. Thirty years of everything.

**After the win**

> _In the lost-and-found you find an envelope addressed to Dante at iSMOKESHOP, stamped Return to Sender. Inside is a card with a heron on it._ **[Clue: Returned envelope]**
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-greet)_: Dante. He painted the mural for our kids’ program and signed it in letters nobody can read. On purpose, he says.

**Rewards:** 80 credits, 100 XP, clue: Returned envelope.

**Field notes:**

- **Bald eagles** (wildlife): Bald eagles nest along the Rappahannock. The Chesapeake Bay region, which the river feeds, has one of the largest bald eagle populations on the Atlantic coast. _Source: Center for Conservation Biology, William & Mary._

### 2.5 End of Shift (finale)

**Game:** war against Sophia. **Objective:** Finale: win War against Sophia. **Table:** eastern_woodlands deck on rappahannock_riverside, deal 2001 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Sophia** _(cards-deal)_: End of shift. One game of War. Loser writes up the man with the phone on a stick.

**After the win**

> **Sophia** _(portrait-neutral)_: People talk about this river like its history ended in 1776. Downriver, the Rappahannock Tribe got land at Fones Cliffs back in 2022.
>
> **Sophia**: It’s still being written. So is this. One mark found. I’ll watch the river; you watch that card.

**Rewards:** 130 credits, 160 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **The river’s name** (history): The river shares its name with the Rappahannock people. The Rappahannock Tribe, based in Virginia’s Northern Neck, was federally recognized in 2018. In 2022 it reacquired 465 acres at Fones Cliffs, a sacred site on the river. _Source: Rappahannock Tribe; U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs; U.S. Department of the Interior._

**Departure**

> **Sophia** _(portrait-think)_: Somebody mailed Dante a heron card, and it came back to a station that never sent it. I don’t like being somebody’s return address.
>
> **Sophia**: Go see him. If you run into the man with the phone on a stick, tell him the sign-in sheets are city records. He can ask for them properly.
>
> _You fold the map into your pocket and set off for Dante’s shop._

**Chapter rewards:** board: rappahannock_riverside, deck: eastern_woodlands, passport stamp (Rappahannock River Station), 350 credits, 230 XP.

**Chapter notes:**

- **About the Eastern Woodlands deck** (about the story): The Eastern Woodlands deck is a visual theme: the wildlife, plants and rivers of the region. The clues and mysteries in this story are fiction; they do not represent Native spirituality or traditions.

## Chapter 3: Neon Commission

**Place:** iSMOKESHOP (fictional). **Host:** Dante. **Cast:** Dante. **Music:** minimal-parlor-loop.

_Dante has been paid, in one-dollar bills, to paint George Washington as thirteen neon monsters._

**The mystery so far:** A client signing only “G. W.” paid Dante in one-dollar bills to paint George Washington as thirteen neon monsters. Under black light, the client’s reference sketch hides the second mark — a heart — and the payments trace back to the card-case maker Jak Gold uses.

**Arrival**

> _You push open the door of iSMOKESHOP. Behind the glass counter, every inch of wall is covered in neon monsters with too many eyes._
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-greet)_: Hey. Lighters are on the left, the art’s on the walls, and I’m behind on a deadline. Which one are you here for?
>
> _You set the returned envelope on the counter. Dante goes quiet, then laughs once._
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-surprise)_: My heron card. I mailed that to a P.O. box that doesn’t exist, with the River Station as the return address. I was painting their mural that week.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-talk)_: The client paid in advance, asked for that card back, then stopped answering. I’m still on design one of thirteen. I finish what I’m paid for.
>
> **Dante** _(cards-fan)_: Help me clear the sketch pile and I’ll show you the brief. Strangest job I’ve taken, and I once painted a lizard wizard on a food truck.

### 3.1 Monster Sketches

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 1. **Table:** dantes_world deck on artists_studio, deal 1013 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _Dante drops a stack of monster sketches on the counter, sorted into suits that do not exist. You start sorting them into real ones._
>
> **Dante** _(cards-shuffle)_: Real suits, aces up. Chaos goes on the paper, not the desk.

**After the win**

> _Under the last sketch you find an order form, typed and paid in advance. The client is listed only as “G. W.”_ **[Clue: Anonymous commission form]**
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-talk)_: Thirteen card designs. George Washington as a neon monster. Paid in one-dollar bills — so, technically, paid in George Washington.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-think)_: I thought it was a bit. Bits don’t usually pay in advance.

**Rewards:** 55 credits, 75 XP, clue: Anonymous commission form.

**Field notes:**

- **Colours that glow** (history): Daylight fluorescent paint — the colours that blaze under a black light on 1960s posters — was developed in the 1930s by brothers Bob and Joe Switzer, who went on to found the Day-Glo company. _Source: American Chemical Society, National Historic Chemical Landmarks._

### 3.2 Colour Clash

**Game:** war against Dante. **Objective:** Win War against Dante. **Table:** dantes_world deck on artists_studio, deal 2026 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Dante** _(cards-deal)_: War. My deck against your deck. Both of them are my deck; I lent you one. Don’t bend the cards.

**After the win**

> **Dante** _(portrait-talk)_: Those sixties Fillmore posters? The lettering melts into the shapes. You can’t skim them. You stand there until the picture resolves.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-think)_: This brief is like that. It isn’t random. Your eyes just haven’t found the rhythm yet.

**Rewards:** 65 credits, 85 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **Posters you have to read slowly** (history): In the mid-1960s, San Francisco concert posters — such as Wes Wilson’s for the Fillmore Auditorium — used swirling hand lettering that was hard to read on purpose, so people stopped to look. _Source: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco._

### 3.3 The Commission

**Game:** go-fish against Dante. **Objective:** Collect 3 books: choose your asks and remember the replies. **Table:** dantes_world deck on artists_studio, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> _Dante pulls out the client’s reference sketch for you: a stiff, old-fashioned portrait of George Washington holding a hand of cards._
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-doubt)_: The brief says “capture my vigor.” My vigor. Clients don’t usually write about themselves like they’re a statue.

**After the win**

> _Dante hands you his first finished design: General Monsterton, a three-eyed George Washington in neon blue, holding twelve cards. The thirteenth card in his hand is blank._ **[Clue: General Monsterton]**
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-greet)_: Keep that one. Proof I was hired before this got strange. And proof I hit at least one deadline.

**Rewards:** 75 credits, 95 XP, clue: General Monsterton.

### 3.4 Monster Pond

**Game:** go-fish against Dante. **Objective:** Win Go Fish against Dante. **Table:** dantes_world deck on artists_studio, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Dante** _(cards-deal)_: Paint’s curing. Go Fish while it does. Rush fluorescent paint and it dries dull.

**After the win**

> **Dante** _(portrait-talk)_: People hear “psychedelic” and think drug joke. The poster artists were working on perception — what your eye does when a pattern won’t sit still.
>
> **Dante** _(full-gesture-a)_: And it was a scene. Printers, bands, kids lining up for a poster. Art made for a room full of people. That’s the part I want.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-doubt)_: Freemasons, though? No idea. The little red hats? No, that’s the Shriners. I think.

**Rewards:** 85 credits, 105 XP.

### 3.5 The Hidden Heart (finale)

**Game:** spider. **Objective:** Finale: clear one-suit Spider. **Table:** dantes_world deck on artists_studio, deal 1003 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _Dante studies the reference sketch, then kills the lights and switches on a black light. You watch him tilt the paper toward it._
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-think)_: The cuff lace is wrong. Lace repeats, and this breaks its rhythm. Look at the gaps, not the threads. Figure and ground.

**After the win**

> _Under the black light, a heart glows in the gaps of Washington’s lace cuff, drawn in invisible ink. It is the exact size of your card’s second blank corner._ **[Clue: The heart mark]**
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-surprise)_: There. Negative space first, fluorescent ink to prove it. Whoever drew this knew exactly how people look at lace: they don’t.

**Rewards:** 140 credits, 170 XP, clue: The heart mark.

**Departure**

> **Dante** _(portrait-think)_: The ones came packed in a custom card case with the maker’s stamp. Same maker Jak Gold uses. He mentions it in roughly every video.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-greet)_: Jak has a back room off Caroline Street. Ring light, tripod, opinions. He’s better than his thumbnails. Don’t tell him I said that.
>
> _You tuck the glowing sketch away with the card. Two corners marked, two to go._

**Chapter rewards:** deck: cannabis_nugs, deck: dantes_world, board: artists_studio, passport stamp (iSMOKESHOP), 400 credits, 260 XP.

**Chapter notes:**

- **About this chapter** (about the story): Dante’s chapter happens at his art counter and is about his artwork. The anonymous commission, the client and the hidden heart are invented for the story.

## Chapter 4: On the Record

**Place:** Jak’s Backroom Card Parlor (fictional). **Host:** Jak Gold. **Cast:** Jak Gold. **Music:** high-roller.

_Jak has filmed, filed and flourished his way to a reply nobody meant him to read._

**The mystery so far:** Jak’s public-records request came back almost entirely redacted, except for one name: Operation Thirteenth Hand. A receipt shows “G. W.” sent a custom card case to an unmarked office, and Jak’s slow-motion footage reveals the third mark — a diamond hidden in the card’s edge.

**Arrival**

> _You knock on a back-room door off Caroline Street. A ring light snaps on in your face. So does a camera._
>
> **Jak Gold**: This is my studio, so you’re on camera. Say the word and it goes off. Most people don’t say the word. They wave.
>
> **Jak Gold**: Dante sent you? Dante texted me eleven monster emojis. I inferred.
>
> _You show Jak the card. He stops talking, which, you sense, is rare._
>
> **Jak Gold**: That card is in my records request. I’m cutting that video tonight, and I need someone who isn’t my audience. Deal in. I think better with my hands busy.

### 4.1 Rolling

**Game:** war against Jak Gold. **Objective:** Win War against Jak Gold. **Table:** jak_gold deck on backroom_card_table, deal 2030 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Jak Gold**: War. Pure chance, so nobody watching can say I cheated. Rolling.

**After the win**

> **Jak Gold**: Six months ago I asked the city, in writing, about “unexplained activity” in the old cellars downtown. State FOIA. Cheap question. Weird answer.
>
> **Jak Gold**: Then I filmed lobbies, your ranger’s included, on her lunch break. Legal, probably. Useful, no. I cut that footage. She was right.

**Rewards:** 60 credits, 80 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **Cardistry** (about the story): Cardistry is the performance art of card flourishes — cuts, spins, springs and fans done for their beauty, not to fool anyone. Unlike magic, it hides nothing. It grew into a worldwide community through online videos.

### 4.2 Three-Card Draw

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 3. **Table:** jak_gold deck on backroom_card_table, deal 1010 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _Jak hands you three practice decks shuffled together and asks you to sort them while he rehearses a one-handed cut._
>
> **Jak Gold**: Three at a time. Same as records: you don’t get to pick which ones come up.

**After the win**

> _Among Jak’s paperwork you find a receipt for a custom card case, ordered from his own card-case maker by a customer who signed as “G. W.”_ **[Clue: Card-case receipt]**
>
> **Jak Gold**: G. W. My case maker remembers him: paid in ones, every bill the same face. That’s one source. I don’t run anything on one source.
>
> **Jak Gold**: Two cases. One to Dante’s shop, full of ones, and Dante confirms it. One to an office above a shuttered storefront, no name on the door. Two sources. Now it’s a lead.

**Rewards:** 70 credits, 90 XP, clue: Card-case receipt.

### 4.3 Public Records

**Game:** go-fish against Jak Gold. **Objective:** Lay down 3 books against Jak Gold. **Table:** jak_gold deck on backroom_card_table, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Jak Gold**: Go Fish. You ask, I disclose. Or I don’t. Like a government agency.

**After the win**

> _Jak switches the camera off before he spreads out the reply for you. Whole paragraphs are blacked out. One phrase survived: OPERATION THIRTEENTH HAND._ **[Clue: Redacted records reply]**
>
> **Jak Gold**: Off camera, because it isn’t content until I know what it is. They redacted everything but the name. Sloppy, or meant to be read.

**Rewards:** 80 credits, 100 XP, clue: Redacted records reply.

**Field notes:**

- **Freedom of Information** (history): The federal Freedom of Information Act became law in 1966. It covers federal agencies, which may withhold information under nine exemptions — one reason released records arrive with black bars. A Virginia city answers under the state’s own Act, which has its own exclusions. _Source: FOIA.gov (U.S. Department of Justice); Virginia FOIA Council._

### 4.4 Redacted

**Game:** go-fish against Jak Gold. **Objective:** Collect 3 books: choose your asks and remember the replies. **Table:** jak_gold deck on backroom_card_table, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Jak Gold**: Every black bar has a width. Measure the gaps and you can guess at the words. Guess, not know. That goes in the video too.
>
> _You read the reply line by line while Jak measures black bars with a steel ruler._

**After the win**

> **Jak Gold**: What made it through: “four marks,” “waterfront,” and “thirteenth hand — not concluded.” Whatever it was, nobody closed the file.

**Rewards:** 90 credits, 110 XP.

### 4.5 Slow Motion (finale)

**Game:** spider. **Objective:** Finale: clear one-suit Spider. **Table:** jak_gold deck on backroom_card_table, deal 3415 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Jak Gold**: Let me borrow the card. One flourish: spring, cascade, catch. My phone shoots two hundred and forty frames a second.
>
> _You hand Jak the card. It flies between his hands with fifty-two others and lands back on top of the deck._

**After the win**

> _Jak plays the footage back for you frame by frame. As the card bends mid-spring, a diamond shows inside its edge — printed so it appears only when the card flexes._ **[Clue: The diamond mark]**
>
> **Jak Gold**: Edge work. Old cheats marked card edges to read them from the side. This one marks itself for whoever bends it right.
>
> **Jak Gold**: Best footage I’ve ever shot. It stays off the channel until we know what it means.

**Rewards:** 150 credits, 180 XP, clue: The diamond mark.

**Departure**

> **Jak Gold**: Three corners: club, heart, diamond. The spade is behind that unmarked door; I’d bet my best deck on it. The building manager banned me from the stairwell. You aren’t banned.
>
> **Jak Gold**: I’m not coming with you. I’ll be here, cutting a video that’s honest and a little boring. You can tell it’s honest because it’s boring.
>
> _You leave Jak rewatching his footage and head for the door with no name on it._

**Chapter rewards:** deck: yummyhole_standard, deck: jak_gold, board: jak_golds_casino, passport stamp (Jak’s Backroom Card Parlor), achievement: halfway-home, 450 credits, 280 XP.

## Chapter 5: Operation Thirteenth Hand

**Place:** Mrs. Gray’s Intelligence Safehouse (fictional). **Host:** Mrs. Gray. **Cast:** Mrs. Gray. **Music:** safehouse-pulse.

_A woman with no first name, a dossier with no happy ending, and a legend somebody borrowed._

**The mystery so far:** In the story, Operation Thirteenth Hand was a fictional 1962 investigation of a phantom card game in the cellars, using a local legend — a game George Washington never finished — as its cover. It was compartmentalized: surveyors photographed the marks, a Freemason from Lodge No. 4 read the history, and nobody saw the whole file. Mrs. Gray inherited it, treats it as a record of what people feared rather than proof, and lets you break the seal no one in her office was cleared to break: the ace of spades holding the fourth mark.

**Arrival**

> _You climb the stairs above the shuttered storefront. The door with no name opens before you can knock._
>
> **Mrs. Gray** _(portrait-neutral)_: You’re late. Not by the clock. By the file.
>
> **Mrs. Gray** _(portrait-doubt)_: Three days ago a card case arrived here, signed “G. W.” I don’t receive packages. I receive explanations. Who is G. W.?
>
> _You show her the card with its three marked corners. She studies it without touching it._
>
> **Mrs. Gray** _(portrait-think)_: A club from the river. A heart from a painter’s commission. A diamond from somebody’s footage. You’ve been busy, and you’ve been noticed.
>
> **Mrs. Gray** _(portrait-doubt)_: Sit. The Hardigan boys had that chair once. Their questions improved after the first hour. Most people’s do.

## Chapter 6: Square and Compasses

**Place:** Fredericksburg Masonic Lodge No. 4 (real). **Host:** Steve Gonzales. **Cast:** Steve Gonzales, Sophia. **Music:** sanctum-pulse.

_Steve Gonzales separates what happened at the lodge in 1752 from what someone invented later._

**The mystery so far:** Steve separates documented history (Washington’s initiation here in 1752, the Capitol cornerstone, the Culper Ring) from the story’s legend. Masons explain the square, compasses, level and plumb as lessons in conduct; suit lore belongs to tarot and other traditions, and the card’s cipher is not Masonic. With compasses, Sophia’s map and the dossier’s survey, he reads the order the card was made to be set in — spade, diamond, heart, club, downstream — and raking light raises two words from the ledger’s blank line: KENMORE — ASK MOTHER.

**Arrival**

> _You stop outside Fredericksburg Masonic Lodge No. 4. A tall man in a dark coat is waiting on the steps with a camera bag and a very old book._
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-greet)_: You must be the one with the card. Steve Gonzales. Mrs. Gray called. She doesn’t call. She lets you find out she knew.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: Ground rules. This lodge is real. George Washington was made a Mason here on November 4, 1752. He was twenty.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-think)_: Your card, the legend, the cipher: none of that is Masonic. Today I show you exactly where the history stops and the story starts.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(cards-reveal)_: And then, I think, which order those suits go in. Vamos.

### 6.1 Cornerstone

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 1. **Table:** freemasonry deck on masonic_lodge_no4, deal 1021 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: A cornerstone is the first stone you build on. Washington laid the Capitol’s in 1793, in a Masonic ceremony. Documented. Now lay yours.

**After the win**

> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-neutral)_: Our working tools are builders’ tools. Masons use them to talk about conduct. The square: deal fairly. The compasses: know your limits.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-doubt)_: Lodges explain them a little differently. That’s normal. A symbol that means only one thing is a label.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-doubt)_: Four suits as four elements is tarot, a different tradition. A secret Masonic card ritual is nobody’s. Your cipher is borrowed costume.

**Rewards:** 70 credits, 90 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **The Capitol cornerstone** (history): On September 18, 1793, George Washington laid the cornerstone of the United States Capitol in a ceremony conducted by Freemasons. _Source: Architect of the Capitol._
- **The working tools** (history): Freemasons explain their builders’ tools as lessons in conduct. One Grand Lodge’s public summary gives the square as morality, the level as equality and the plumb as upright living. An 18th-century text says the compasses keep us “within bounds.” Readings vary between lodges. _Source: Grand Lodge of California, “Fellow Craft Working Tools” (freemason.org); Grand Lodge of British Columbia and Yukon, “The Working Tools”._

### 6.2 Level and Plumb

**Game:** war against Steve Gonzales. **Objective:** Win War against Steve Gonzales. **Table:** freemasonry deck on masonic_lodge_no4, deal 2021 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Steve Gonzales** _(cards-shuffle)_: The level is about meeting as equals. War is the most level game there is. Nobody gets to be clever. Including me. Especially me.

**After the win**

> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: The plumb is the other half: upright when nobody’s checking. In VFX, if your verticals lean, the audience feels it before they can say why.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-neutral)_: Before media work, I studied at Norwich, the oldest private military college in the country. Intelligence history sticks to you.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-think)_: Washington ran real spies: the Culper Ring, a code book, invisible ink. If he’d wanted to hide something, four suits on a card would be beneath him.

**Rewards:** 80 credits, 100 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **Norwich University** (history): Norwich University in Vermont, founded in 1819 by Captain Alden Partridge, is the oldest private military college in the United States and is recognized as the birthplace of ROTC. _Source: Norwich University._

### 6.3 Sources

**Game:** go-fish against Steve Gonzales, Sophia. **Objective:** Lay down 3 books against Steve and Sophia. **Table:** freemasonry deck on masonic_lodge_no4, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> _The door opens behind you and Sophia walks in, carrying a pencil and a look you recognise._
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-doubt)_: Mrs. Gray says you’re consulting a Freemason. I’m here to check his footnotes.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-greet)_: Ranger. Welcome. Please check everything.

**After the win**

> **Sophia** _(portrait-think)_: His dates are right. His sources are real. I hate it a little.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-greet)_: Nobody has asked for my bibliography in years. I’m moved.
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-neutral)_: Don’t be. Where did you learn to cite like that?
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: The lodge, mostly. And Burning Man. You build something huge with strangers, then write down who did what, so next year’s crew can find it.
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-greet)_: That’s a trail inventory.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-think)_: “Everyone is invited to work. Everyone is invited to play.” Their words, not mine. A good lodge night isn’t so different.

**Rewards:** 90 credits, 110 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **The real “Masonic cipher”** (history): The pigpen cipher, which swaps letters for shapes taken from a grid, was used by some Freemasons in the 1700s and is often called the Masonic cipher. It is publicly documented — and it uses no playing cards. _Source: Scottish Rite Masonic Museum & Library._
- **The red hats** (history): The red fez Dante remembered belongs to the Shriners, a fraternity whose members are Freemasons. Since 1922 the Shriners have run a network of children’s hospitals. _Source: Shriners International; Shriners Children’s._

Everyone is invited to play.” Communal Effort values creative cooperation and collaboration. _Source: Burning Man Project, “The 10 Principles” (burningman.org)._

**Chapter notes:**

- **History and story** (about the story): Washington’s initiation at the Fredericksburg lodge in 1752 is documented history. The card, its suit cipher, the legend and the lodge’s part in the mystery are invented for the story. Reading the four suits as elements comes from tarot and other esoteric traditions, not Freemasonry; no secret card ceremony is a real Masonic practice; and the card’s glow is this game’s own magic.

## Chapter 7: A Mother’s Opinion

**Place:** Kenmore (real). **Host:** Mary Ball Washington. **Cast:** Mary Ball Washington. **Music:** kenmore-manor-theme.

_At her daughter’s house, Mary Ball Washington’s ghost has a few things to say about her son._

**The mystery so far:** At Kenmore — her daughter Betty’s house, not hers — Mary Ball Washington’s ghost tells her version of the legend: twelve hands of cards with her son, scored in her own ledger, and George walking away before the thirteenth because he was losing. A widow who kept the accounts of a farm for nearly thirty years, she wants the ledger closed honestly, not won. She confirms Steve’s reading, seals a letter for George and gives you the iron key to the cellar door where he waits.

**Arrival**

> _You step into Kenmore’s parlor. Sculpted plaster leaves bloom across the ceiling above you. Beneath it, a woman in a lace cap is already seated at the card table._
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-neutral)_: You are standing on my daughter’s floor. Wipe your feet.
>
> _You show her the card and the ledger’s last line. She does not look surprised._
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-talk)_: “Ask Mother.” Of course he wrote that. A grown man, a general, a president, and still sending people to ask Mother.
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-doubt)_: Before we go on: I did not live here. This was Betty’s house — Betty and Fielding’s. Mine was on Charles Street, a short walk away. Do get it right.
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(cards-deal)_: People mix the two houses up because it makes a tidier story. I have had quite enough tidy stories about this family. Sit.

**After the win**

**Field notes:**

- **The Fredericksburg gunnery** (history): During the Revolutionary War, Fielding Lewis helped run the Fredericksburg Gun Manufactory to arm Virginia’s troops, spending much of his own fortune on it. _Source: George Washington Foundation (Kenmore)._
- **The people on Betty’s list** (history): Historic Kenmore’s researchers trace the community the Lewises enslaved through four surviving documents, including a 1782 list in Betty Lewis’s hand. One man there, Billy, was 38 that year, and was probably the head of the household staff. _Source: George Washington Foundation, “Billy at the Door” (kenmore.org)._

>

**After the win**

> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: Jak reads cards. I read history. Dante reads… what, exactly?
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-think)_: Figure and ground. Stare at bricks long enough and one patch stops being wall. That patch is a door.
>
> _You look where Dante is pointing. Behind a curtain of roots is a door with four empty sockets, each shaped like a suit._

**Rewards:** 90 credits, 110 XP.

### 8.3 Echoes

**Game:** war against Jak Gold. **Objective:** Win War against Jak Gold. **Table:** inspire deck on underground_tunnels, deal 2024 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Jak Gold**: While Steve measures the door: War. Best way I know to stop thinking about the ceiling.

**After the win**

> **Jak Gold**: My theory: the door wants new deck order. Spades, diamonds, clubs, hearts. Every fresh deck comes out of the box that way.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-doubt)_: Your theory has a factory in it. That door is older than the factory.
>
> **Jak Gold**: Noted. Disagreed. Filed.

**Rewards:** 100 credits, 120 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **New deck order** (history): Bicycle decks from the United States Playing Card Company come sealed in “new deck order”: ace to king of spades, ace to king of diamonds, then king to ace of clubs and king to ace of hearts. Magicians and cardists rely on it. _Source: United States Playing Card Company (Bicycle)._

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 3. **Table:** inspire deck on underground_tunnels, deal 1018 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **Dante** _(portrait-talk)_: My markers are fading. Quick — follow the arrows before they stop believing in us.

> _Dante hands you the sketch he has been drawing all the way down: a glowing map of every turn, with a small monster waving at each one._ **[Clue: Dante’s tunnel map]**

### 8.5 The Four-Suit Door (finale)

**Game:** spider. **Objective:** Finale: set the four marks, then clear one-suit Spider. **Table:** inspire deck on underground_tunnels, deal 1001 (verified winnable).

**Before**

>
> **Jak Gold**: Club from the river, heart from Dante’s brief, diamond from my footage, spade from Mrs. Gray’s file. Everybody brought one.

**Puzzle:** _You hold the card to the door. In which order do you set the four marks?_ Answer: spades, diamonds, hearts, clubs.

**Hints after each wrong try (the last repeats)**

> **Jak Gold**: Didn’t budge. New deck order, maybe? Spades, diamonds, clubs, hearts. Works on every deck I’ve ever opened.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-think)_: What about the order you found them in? Club, heart, diamond, spade? Or is that backwards… oh.
>

>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: Spade, diamond, heart, club. Downstream from the north. Trust the river.

## Chapter 9: The Thirteenth Hand

**Place:** Washington’s Spectral Card Parlor (supernatural). **Host:** George Washington’s Ghost. **Cast:** George Washington’s Ghost, Mary Ball Washington. **Music:** esoteric-order-loop.

_George Washington’s ghost has waited a very long time to finish this game. He does not plan to lose it._

**The mystery so far:** The legend resolves: George Washington’s ghost — who planted the card, sketched the heron and commissioned Dante, all to lure a challenger — has waited to play the thirteenth hand he walked away from. Every portrait flatters him; one ledger, in his mother’s hand, says he left. You win it, his mother’s letter turns the loss into a debt paid, and the card awakens with all four corners filled.

**Arrival**

> _You step into a card room that should not fit under the town. The candles burn without shrinking. At the head of the table, a tall ghost in a blue coat rises to meet you._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-greet)_: At last! A challenger! Do you know how long I have waited? Two hundred and — never mind how long.
>
> _You show him General Monsterton, Dante’s three-eyed neon portrait of him._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-surprise)_: Three eyes. Magnificent. Precisely the vigor I asked for. I look as though I could win at anything.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-think)_: Yes, it was I. The card in Lot 13, the heron, the commission. A general recruits. Twelve hands were played in my mother’s parlor. I was called away before the thirteenth.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(cards-signature)_: They have written a great deal about me. Most of it flattering. One ledger is not, and it is in my mother’s hand.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(cards-signature)_: Tonight we finish it. Five games. I intend to win all five, and to be remembered winning them.

### 9.1 The General’s Welcome

**Game:** war against George Washington’s Ghost. **Objective:** Win War against George Washington’s ghost. **Table:** washington_ghost deck on washington_final_table, deal 2035 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(cards-deal)_: We begin with War. I have some experience. Most of it was losing, until it wasn’t.

**After the win**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-doubt)_: A warm-up. I allowed you that. It was strategy. I was famous for strategy. Look it up. Not the losses. The strategy.

**Rewards:** 85 credits, 105 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **The Delaware crossing** (history): On the night of December 25–26, 1776, Washington led his army across the icy Delaware River and surprised the Hessian garrison at Trenton the next morning. _Source: George Washington’s Mount Vernon._

### 9.2 Spectral Draw

**Game:** klondike. **Objective:** Complete Klondike, Draw 3. **Table:** washington_ghost deck on washington_final_table, deal 3200 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> _The cards deal themselves in front of you, three at a time, drifting into place like snow._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-talk)_: Patience. A soldier’s game. The winter at Valley Forge was mostly patience. And soup.

**After the win**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-think)_: Hm. You are steadier than my generals. Do not tell them I said so. They are also ghosts, and they gossip.

**Rewards:** 95 credits, 115 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **Valley Forge** (history): The Continental Army camped at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, through the winter of 1777–78. Baron von Steuben drilled the troops there, and the army marched out in June 1778 better trained. _Source: National Park Service, Valley Forge National Historical Park._

### 9.3 The Twelfth Hand

**Game:** go-fish against George Washington’s Ghost. **Objective:** Collect 3 books: choose your asks and remember the replies. **Table:** washington_ghost deck on washington_final_table, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> _You recognise the deal in front of you: the twelfth hand from the ledger, laid out exactly as it was written._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-doubt)_: Mother kept that ledger. Mother keeps everything. Including accounts I would prefer were closed.

**After the win**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-surprise)_: You solved the twelfth hand. I lost that one, originally. I maintain the candle was in my eyes.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-think)_: Every portrait of me has a fine coat and a certain look. Not one shows me leaving a card table early. She was the only one who wrote that down.

**Rewards:** 105 credits, 125 XP.

### 9.4 No Retreat

**Game:** spider. **Objective:** Clear one-suit Spider. **Table:** washington_ghost deck on washington_final_table, deal 3400 (verified winnable).

**Before**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-neutral)_: Spider. A long game, and no retreat. I am, historically, a great believer in a well-timed retreat. Not tonight.

**After the win**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-doubt)_: Four games to you. This is becoming —
>
> _A cold draft crosses the room. Every candle leans toward the door behind you._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-surprise)_: Mother?

**Rewards:** 115 credits, 135 XP.

**Field notes:**

- **A famous retreat** (history): After losing the Battle of Long Island in August 1776, Washington moved his whole army across the East River to Manhattan in a single night, hidden by darkness and fog. _Source: George Washington’s Mount Vernon._

### 9.5 The Thirteenth Hand (finale)

**Game:** go-fish against George Washington’s Ghost. **Objective:** Finale: win the thirteenth hand against George Washington’s ghost. **Table:** washington_ghost deck on washington_final_table, a fresh deal each try at an Easy table.

**Before**

> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-neutral)_: Don’t stop on my account, George. I’m only here to watch you finish something.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-doubt)_: Mother. You look… well. Considering.
>
> _You lay the Thirteenth Hand card face up in the middle of the table. All four of its corners are marked._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(cards-signature)_: Thirteen ranks, thirteen books. Whoever lays down more wins the thirteenth hand — and the card.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-think)_: And this time the ledger records how it ended. Not how I left.

**After the win**

> _You lay down your last book. The Thirteenth Hand card begins to glow at all four corners: spade, diamond, heart and club._ **[Clue: The awakened card]**
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-surprise)_: I demand a recount. And a rematch. And —
>
> _You hand George the letter from his mother. He reads the back, and goes quiet._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-doubt)_: “You owe me a hand.” …I suppose I did. Longer than I have owed anyone anything.
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-greet)_: Well played. Both of you. Mostly the one who is alive.
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-talk)_: Write it down, George. Lost the thirteenth hand, and stayed to the end. It reads better than you think.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-think)_: Lost, and stayed. Very well. Two centuries of sulking, concluded. I feel… lighter. Which, for a ghost, is saying something.

**Rewards:** 220 credits, 260 XP, clue: The awakened card.

**Departure**

> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(portrait-greet)_: Keep the card. It is finished now, as the game is. And take my deck. I shan’t need it until the rematch.
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(cards-signature)_: There will be a rematch.
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-doubt)_: There will be a nap, George.
>
> _The candles go out together. When your eyes adjust, you are standing in an empty cellar, holding a card that glows faintly at the corners._

**Chapter rewards:** deck: washington_ghost, board: washington_final_table, passport stamp (Washington’s Spectral Card Parlor), achievement: chronicles-complete, 800 credits, 400 XP.

**Chapter notes:**

- **About the legend** (about the story): Washington really did play cards and record his winnings and losses. The unfinished game, the ghosts, the card and the spectral parlor are a legend invented for this story.

## Epilogue: Not for Sale

**After the thirteenth hand**

> _A week later, you bring the card back to Cheryl’s shop, where it all began. It sits under the lamp in a frame nobody can afford._
>
> **Cheryl** _(portrait-doubt)_: Provenance: one ghost, four witnesses and a receipt for everything. Best file I’ve ever written. The sign says NOT FOR SALE. DON’T ASK.
>
> **Sophia** _(portrait-greet)_: The heron’s still at the bend. I logged her this morning. Some things are allowed to stay a mystery. The sign-in sheets are not among them.
>
> **Dante** _(portrait-surprise)_: All thirteen monster cards are done! The client paid the final invoice. In ones. Obviously.
>
> **Jak Gold**: My video’s up: “I Have No Footage of a Ghost (Proof).” The camera was off for the good part. The comments are about my flourish anyway.
>
> **Mrs. Gray** _(portrait-neutral)_: File closed. Reason: concluded. I’ve wanted to type that word for a very long time. Under sources, I put your name. Don’t frame it.
>
> **Steve Gonzales** _(portrait-talk)_: I’ve added a page to the lodge’s research: history in one column, legend in the other. Sophia approved it. Twice.
>
> _On your way out, you find an envelope on the counter, sealed in blue wax. Inside are a single dollar bill and a note in a very confident hand._
>
> **George Washington’s Ghost** _(cards-signature)_: Best of thirteen? — G. W.
>
> _Under his signature, in a smaller and much firmer hand, someone has added a line for you._
>
> **Mary Ball Washington** _(portrait-talk)_: He will lose again. Do keep score. — M. W.
>
> _You smile. Somewhere under the town, a candle lights itself. Ghost rematches are open._

| The Thirteenth Hand | 1 | card | key | An antique playing card with no suit and no rank, titled “The Thirteenth Hand”. Its four corners are blank where suit marks should be. |
| Estate-sale receipt | 1 | document | optional | Cheryl’s receipt for the box: “Lot 13 — one card box, contents as found. Paid in full.” |
| Ledger of twelve hands | 1 | document | key | A leather ledger from the box. Twelve hands of cards are recorded in faded ink; the thirteenth line is blank. |
| River postcard | 1 | document | key | An old postcard of the Rappahannock. Someone has sketched a heron on the back in pencil and written: “River Station.” |
| Field journal page | 2 | document | optional | A page from the station’s wildlife log: the same heron, logged at the same bend of the river, every morning. |
| The club mark | 2 | object | key | A small club (♣) carved into an old trail marker at the heron’s bend. It matches one blank corner of the card exactly. |
| Returned envelope | 2 | document | key | An envelope from the station’s lost-and-found, addressed to Dante at iSMOKESHOP and marked “Return to sender”. Inside: a card with a heron on it. |
| Sophia’s annotated river map | 2 | document | key | Sophia’s own map of the river trail, covered in her field notes. Near the old waterfront, four small marks traced from an older survey are circled in pencil; one of them is a club. |
| Anonymous commission form | 3 | document | key | A typed order for thirteen card designs — George Washington as a neon monster — paid in advance in one-dollar bills and signed only “G. W.” |
| General Monsterton | 3 | card | optional | Dante’s first finished design: a three-eyed, neon-blue George Washington holding twelve cards, with a thirteenth left blank. |
| The heart mark | 3 | object | key | A heart (♥) drawn in invisible ink in the lace cuff of the client’s reference sketch. It shows under black light and fits the card’s second blank corner. |
| Card-case receipt | 4 | document | key | A receipt from Jak’s card-case maker: two custom cases ordered by “G. W.”, paid in ones — one shipped to Dante’s shop, one to an office with no name on the door. |
| Redacted records reply | 4 | document | key | The reply to Jak’s public-records request about the old cellars: almost all black bars. One phrase survives — OPERATION THIRTEENTH HAND — with “four marks”, “waterfront” and “not concluded”. |
| The diamond mark | 4 | recording | key | Jak’s 240-frames-a-second footage of a spring flourish: as the card flexes, a diamond (♦) printed inside its edge shows for a few frames. |
| Operation Thirteenth Hand dossier | 5 | document | key | The fictional operation’s file, opened in 1962: survey photos pin each of the four marks to a spot near the old waterfront. Its cover story was a legend — a card game George Washington never finished. |
| The spade mark | 5 | card | key | The ace of spades that sealed the dossier’s last folder. In its corner is a spade (♠) cut to fit the card’s last blank corner. |
| Steve’s suit-order diagram | 6 | document | key | Steve’s compasses drawing over Sophia’s map and the dossier’s survey: the four marks on the corners of a square, read downstream from the north — spade, diamond, heart, club. Labelled in his hand: “Not Masonic. Borrowed tools.” |
| The thirteenth line | 6 | document | key | Under Steve’s raking light, the ledger’s blank thirteenth line shows words pressed into the paper by a dry pen: KENMORE — ASK MOTHER. |
| Mary’s letter to George | 7 | document | key | A letter sealed by Mary Ball Washington’s ghost. On the front: George. On the back: You owe me a hand. She says to give it to him when he starts to sulk. |
| Iron key | 7 | object | key | A cold iron key from Mary Ball Washington’s ghost. It opens a cellar door on the old waterfront. |
| Dante’s tunnel map | 8 | document | optional | Dante’s glowing sketch of every turn of the tunnels, with a small monster waving at each one. |
| The four-suit door | 8 | object | key | The sealed door under the old town. Set with the four marks — spade, diamond, heart, club — its thirteen tumblers fell from king to ace. |
| The awakened card | 9 | card | key | The Thirteenth Hand card after the final game, glowing at all four corners: spade, diamond, heart and club. The game is finished. |
